title: Language
excerpt: By age 4, most children are already chatty and use multi-word sentences, but their language grows noticeably more sophisticated by age 5. Vocabulary expands from a few hundred or early thousand words at 3-4 years to an active lexicon of several thousand words
html:
Language across ages: 4–5 years · 5–7 years · 7–9 years · 9–12 years · 12–25 years

By age 4, most children are already chatty and use multi-word sentences, but their language grows noticeably more sophisticated by age 5. Vocabulary expands from a few hundred or early thousand words at 3-4 years to an active lexicon of several thousand words by age 5 1. Five-year-olds frequently learn new words through fast-mapping and can name basic colors, shapes, and common objects; they also start using words for more abstract concepts (e.g. words for feelings like "confused", "decide", or "remember", or spatial relations like "between" and "above") 2, 3. Syntax and grammar show clear advancements: a 4-year-old’s sentences often average 4-5 words, whereas a 5-year-old commonly speaks in sentences of 6+ words 4. By 5, children reliably form complex sentences with conjunctions ("and," "because") and even basic subordinate clauses. They begin to use different sentence types; for example, many 5-year-olds can produce in both active and passive sentence constructions to convey the same meaning (e.g. "The dog chased the cat" vs. "The cat was chased by the dog") 2. Grammatical morphemes are largely in place: five-year-olds correctly use plural -s, past -ed, and even comparatives/superlatives (adding -er or -est to adjectives) 2. They still make the occasional overregularization error (saying "runned" or "sheeps"), but such errors become less frequent.

Pragmatic and conversational skills undergo refinement between four and five. Four-year-olds are enthusiastic conversationalists but may provide either too little or too much information when telling a story, and they often assume the listener knows the context. By age 5, children are better at tailoring their language to the listener’s perspective 2. This reflects gains in social cognition that allow a child to, for instance, explain an idea more simply to a younger child or supply relevant background information to an unfamiliar listener. Five-year-olds also improve in turn-taking and narrative coherence. They can recount past events in a (somewhat) logical sequence, and their stories include more details about who was involved, where it happened, and when (e.g. "We went to the park yesterday and my friend Alice and I fed the ducks") 2; by five, many children can narrate a simple setting->problem->resolution storyline and use temporal/causal connectives ("then… because…") and pronoun reference more consistently, reflecting improved coherence and making self-explanation and planning through language feasible. Their storytelling is still imperfect (endings might be abrupt or chronology jumbled) but compared to 4-year-olds, five-year-olds include more temporal and causal language and are beginning to grasp the basics of plot structure 2. A preschool study examines narrative comprehension (Figure) 5. A small study measures language after shared reading (Figure) 6.

Another leap in this period is the understanding of non-literal language and humor. Four-year-olds enjoy silly words and simple jokes, but they often interpret language very literally. By five, many children start to appreciate figurative expressions and wordplay. For example, a 5-year-old might giggle at idioms or understand common metaphors, realizing that "pulling someone’s leg" is a joke and not an act of aggression 1. They also use language socially to tease or tell simple jokes, and they love absurd rhymes or playing with "naughty" words (it’s common for 4-5-year-olds to experiment with so-called "bathroom words" for shock value, reflecting their burgeoning sense of humor). Pragmatically, five-year-olds are learning social conventions of speech: they modulate volume and tone to suit the setting and use more polite forms ("could I have...?") in requests 2. Overall, the typical five-year-old is a confident user of language, being able to carry on extended conversations and narrate events while continuing to use language as a tool for learning (by asking endless "Why?" questions).
